principles.title: Identify the transition that constrains the run
principles.apply: Before selecting the opening, locate the transfer with the fewest viable approaches and plan earlier leaves to support it.
principles.exceptions: A difficult pot and a difficult position transfer are different problems; do not assume the visibly hardest pot is the bottleneck.
principles.check: Which later transfer removes the most options?

principles.title: Track more than one bottleneck
principles.apply: Identify separate early and late constraints so solving the first does not sacrifice the second.
principles.exceptions: Do not force every layout into one key-shot explanation.
principles.check: What must remain possible after the first problem is solved?

principles.title: Count usable pockets before choosing position
principles.apply: When a ball has limited pocket access, work from its feasible pocket and approach region.
principles.exceptions: An apparent opening in a drawing is not a measured clearance.
principles.check: Which pockets remain feasible after accounting for blockers?

principles.title: An easy pot can be a difficult position ball
principles.apply: Treat pocketing ease and the ability to leave the next angle as separate attributes.
principles.exceptions: Do not call a hanging ball an automatic position solution.
principles.check: Can this easy ball actually send the cue ball where it is needed?

principles.title: Open balls still require a connected plan
principles.apply: Evaluate the connections between open balls and the remaining obstacles before declaring a run easy.
principles.exceptions: Do not invent complications where a simple stop-shot chain works.
principles.check: Does each open pot lead to a useful subsequent shot?

principles.title: Recognize an isolated ball as an access problem
principles.apply: Check how the cue ball can enter and leave an isolated ball's area without relying on nearby linking balls.
principles.exceptions: Isolation alone does not prove difficulty; examine available angles and pockets.
principles.check: What shot provides a practical bridge to this area?

principles.title: Work backward through necessary approach angles
principles.apply: Start with a constrained finish or transition, identify its useful approach, and work backward to reachable predecessor leaves.
principles.exceptions: Backward reasoning generates candidates; it does not verify forward reachability.
principles.check: Can the preceding shot reach the required approach without disturbing the plan?

principles.title: Plan the angle on the next ball for the ball after it
principles.apply: Choose a leave that supports the following transfer rather than merely exposing the next pot.
principles.exceptions: The final ball may need no further movement.
principles.check: What can the cue ball do after pocketing the next ball?

principles.title: Use the selected pocket line as a geometric reference
principles.apply: Define the object-ball-to-intended-pocket line and identify the useful cue-ball side relative to the desired continuation.
principles.exceptions: Left and right depend on orientation and pocket choice; never memorize them as universal labels.
principles.check: Which actual side of this selected line supports the route?

principles.title: Cross a pocket line deliberately when the next route needs it
principles.apply: Recognize when an earlier shot must carry the cue ball across a later pocket line to create the necessary departure angle.
principles.exceptions: Crossing too far can replace one unsuitable angle with another.
principles.check: How much crossing preserves a makeable pot and usable departure?

principles.title: Avoid an unintended pocket-line crossing
principles.apply: Treat the pocket line as a boundary when crossing it would reverse or complicate the next route.
principles.exceptions: Another pocket or recovery route may make the other side usable.
principles.check: What continuation is lost if the leave crosses this boundary?

principles.title: Straight position can be the correct objective
principles.apply: Use straight or nearly straight leaves when controlled stop, follow or draw supports the planned sequence.
principles.exceptions: Avoid treating straightness as always good or always bad.
principles.check: Does straight position simplify this transfer or remove needed movement?

principles.title: Preserve a small angle for controlled local movement
principles.apply: Prefer a manageable small angle when only modest lateral travel or a short transfer is needed.
principles.exceptions: A small angle may demand excessive force for a distant transfer.
principles.check: How much angle is sufficient for the actual movement required?

principles.title: Create sufficient angle for a substantial transfer
principles.apply: Set up enough angle to reach a distant region using a controllable stroke and suitable cushions.
principles.exceptions: More angle can increase pot difficulty; do not maximize angle independently.
principles.check: Does the angle reduce forcing without making the pot unreasonably difficult?

principles.title: Reassess route and speed when contact thickness changes
principles.apply: Recognize that a thicker or thinner hit changes cue-ball departure and retained motion; recheck both clearance and distance.
principles.exceptions: Do not infer exact energy transfer from an uncalibrated image.
principles.check: Does the changed cut still clear the blocker and reach the region?

principles.title: Seek a useful region rather than a single stopping point
principles.apply: Judge leaves by the range of positions preserving the next pot and continuation.
principles.exceptions: A drawn region is a hypothesis until its continuations have been checked.
principles.check: Which nearby outcomes remain useful?

principles.title: Prefer an approach that travels along the useful region
principles.apply: Compare travel direction through the landing region; an aligned approach may preserve the angle over a larger stopping range.
principles.exceptions: The aligned route can be worse if its path encounters pockets or blockers.
principles.check: Does short or long travel still leave the intended continuation?

principles.title: Evaluate the consequence of coming up short
principles.apply: Compare routes by the quality of plausible short leaves, not only the ideal endpoint.
principles.exceptions: The tolerable error direction depends on the layout.
principles.check: Does a slightly short leave become straight, blocked or wrong-sided?

principles.title: Evaluate the consequence of going too far
principles.apply: Inspect long leaves for line crossing, lost angle or excess travel after a cushion.
principles.exceptions: Long is not always worse than short; compare actual recovery options.
principles.check: What changes first as the cue ball passes the intended region?

principles.title: Reduce the number of precision-speed demands in a sequence
principles.apply: Compare whole routes by how many transitions depend on narrowly judged stopping distances.
principles.exceptions: A longer route with several sensitive cushion contacts can be worse than a short precise shot.
principles.check: How many shots in this plan require unusually narrow speed control?

principles.title: Exploit a short controlled move when it removes a larger speed demand
principles.apply: Consider a small follow, draw or hold move that preserves the following angle and avoids a delicate longer roll.
principles.exceptions: Short movement is not inherently easier if it needs a very thin cut or awkward stroke.
principles.check: Does this local move simplify both the current and following shot?

principles.title: Include physical cueing room in the useful region
principles.apply: Leave space from a cushion when the next shot requires accessible low contact or a level stroke.
principles.exceptions: A rail-adjacent leave may be suitable for a different stroke or continuation.
principles.check: Can the intended next tip position and stroke be delivered from this leave?

principles.title: Distinguish tip location from cue-ball state at impact
principles.apply: Reason about sliding, rolling or residual backspin at object-ball contact rather than predicting solely from the tip badge.
principles.exceptions: Distance, speed, cloth and initial spin affect the state; exact values need simulation or observation.
principles.check: What spin state is needed when the cue ball reaches the object ball?

principles.title: A low strike need not produce backward travel
principles.apply: Allow below-center contact to create stun or controlled forward/lateral movement when appropriate.
principles.exceptions: Do not promise that every soft low strike kills the ball; impact state and geometry matter.
principles.check: Is the desired outcome draw, stun or reduced forward motion?

principles.title: Retain enough draw to reach contact when draw is needed
principles.apply: Account for travel to the object ball before prescribing a draw-dependent route.
principles.exceptions: A tip diagram alone does not quantify surviving backspin.
principles.check: Will the proposed launch conditions preserve the required backspin at contact?

principles.title: Use the sliding departure as a reference before modifying it
principles.apply: Compare the sliding cue-ball departure with the required route and adjust the impact state when needed.
principles.exceptions: Ideal tangent geometry is a starting approximation, not proof of the full trajectory.
principles.check: Does the sliding route point toward a useful cushion or region?

principles.title: Use stop shots to connect compatible positions
principles.apply: Recognize sequences where holding the cue ball after a pot naturally exposes the next required angle.
principles.exceptions: A stop requires appropriate alignment and impact state; low spin alone does not ensure it.
principles.check: Does holding this position preserve the next shot rather than stall the plan?

principles.title: Use controlled hold shots to preserve a useful nearby angle
principles.apply: Consider limiting cue-ball motion when larger travel would lose an already useful connection.
principles.exceptions: Do not imply that the cue ball can be held arbitrarily on any cut.
principles.check: How much movement is geometrically unavoidable and still acceptable?

principles.title: Use controlled forward travel to create an angle
principles.apply: Use a measured forward move when it deliberately establishes the next useful side or cut.
principles.exceptions: Too much follow can cross the wrong boundary or approach a pocket.
principles.check: What is the acceptable forward range before the angle becomes unhelpful?

principles.title: Use a small draw move to create rather than force an angle
principles.apply: Compare a short backward move with longer position routes when it sets up a manageable continuation.
principles.exceptions: Short draw still depends on distance, stroke access and retained spin.
principles.check: Does the draw distance create the needed angle without excessive precision?

principles.title: Improve the incoming angle before demanding more power
principles.apply: When alternatives are comparable, choose the previous leave that permits controlled motion instead of forcing a poor angle.
principles.exceptions: Some transfers genuinely require speed; soft is not an unconditional objective.
principles.check: Is the force requirement a consequence of an avoidable earlier leave?

principles.title: Use a cushion to reshape the position approach
principles.apply: Compare a cushion-assisted approach with a direct stopping route when the rebound preserves a wider useful range.
principles.exceptions: Cushions add calibration and spin sensitivity; the source's confidence is not a guarantee.
principles.check: Does the rebound improve the region enough to justify extra uncertainty?

principles.title: Treat the cushion contact location as an intermediate target
principles.apply: Connect a feasible cushion-contact region to the desired outgoing direction.
principles.exceptions: A precise diamond or contact point from a diagram is not transferable to an arbitrary table.
principles.check: How wide is the acceptable cushion-contact region?

principles.title: Use running spin for suitable rebound and travel demands
principles.apply: Consider side spin that assists the intended cushion route when angle alone is insufficient.
principles.exceptions: Running spin is defined relative to the cushion approach, not a universal left/right setting.
principles.check: Which rebound and travel changes are needed at each cushion?

principles.title: Avoid running spin that carries the ball beyond position
principles.apply: Compare reduced or absent side spin when extra cushion travel would flatten the next angle or overshoot the region.
principles.exceptions: Do not simply remove spin without checking the changed rebound direction.
principles.check: Does the added spin improve the route or merely increase overrun?

principles.title: Use reverse spin selectively to hold or reshape a rebound
principles.apply: Consider a checking rebound when it helps preserve the required angle and travel distance.
principles.exceptions: Reverse can affect direction and speed together; it is not a universal brake.
principles.check: What useful angle is preserved and what new miss risk is introduced?

principles.title: Use small spin changes to adjust a rebound direction
principles.apply: Consider a modest side-spin adjustment when it corrects the outgoing route without unnecessary extra travel.
principles.exceptions: A small tip change can have a large effect; no fixed percentage follows from qualitative wording.
principles.check: Is the adjustment changing the needed direction, distance or both?

principles.title: Keep multi-rail routes among alternatives
principles.apply: Do not discard a longer cushion route solely because it has more rails; it may provide a natural angle and forgiving approach.
principles.exceptions: Do not prefer extra rails automatically or ignore accumulated error and pocket approaches.
principles.check: Which route has the better combined pot, path and continuation margin?

principles.title: Choose order by connections rather than isolated pot ease
principles.apply: In order-choice play, compare how one ball's leave makes another accessible and preserves the finish.
principles.exceptions: Rotation first-contact requirements restrict these choices.
principles.check: Which order creates the simplest chain of feasible transfers?

principles.title: Use a good opportunity to address a restricted ball
principles.apply: Consider resolving a ball while a useful approach or predecessor remains available.
principles.exceptions: Hardest-first is not a rule; a linking shot may be needed before the problem ball.
principles.check: What useful access disappears if this ball is deferred?

principles.title: A problem ball may be appropriate late or last
principles.apply: Allow a restricted ball later when the preceding chain reaches it well and it provides a workable finish.
principles.exceptions: Deferring the problem is justified only by a feasible approach and exit.
principles.check: Why does delaying this ball improve the complete chain?

principles.title: The ball nearest the winner need not be the key ball
principles.apply: Select the final object ball by reachable approach and useful exit to the winner, not distance alone.
principles.exceptions: A nearby ball can still be excellent if the required leave is accessible.
principles.check: Can the candidate key ball be reached and used without a fragile transfer?

principles.title: Plan access to the winning ball before committing to order
principles.apply: Choose a feasible finish and arrange the final predecessor and its incoming angle accordingly.
principles.exceptions: An attractive finish is insufficient if the opening cannot connect to it.
principles.check: Which earlier shot establishes the key ball's useful angle?

principles.title: Remove a pocket obstruction as a prerequisite
principles.apply: Recognize when another ball must be removed to open a needed pocket or position route.
principles.exceptions: Removing a ball may also remove a useful connection; check the complete updated layout.
principles.check: What access opens and what option disappears after the clearance?

principles.title: Limit unnecessary movement when connections remain sound
principles.apply: Compare compact controlled chains against larger transfers when their finish and risk are comparable.
principles.exceptions: Shortest total distance alone does not establish the best pattern.
principles.check: Can the same useful angles be retained with less demanding movement?

principles.title: Preserve awareness of opponent balls throughout the route
principles.apply: Account for opponent balls blocking pots and cue-ball corridors even when all own balls are open.
principles.exceptions: Do not assume an opponent ball stays untouched if the simulated path contacts it.
principles.check: Does each transfer retain a clear path around the remaining balls?

principles.title: Reconsider the next pocket when the leave differs
principles.apply: Compare another legal pocket when it gives a better continuation from the actual leave.
principles.exceptions: A pocket switch changes its reference line and all downstream angles.
principles.check: Does the new pocket restore a workable chain?

principles.title: Keep more than one continuation for plausible leaves
principles.apply: Describe recovery branches tied to observed angle or position rather than blindly repeating the nominal controls.
principles.exceptions: A recovery suggestion remains provisional until tested from that actual state.
principles.check: Which branch matches the cue ball's actual position?

principles.title: An intentional secondary contact can be a recovery option
principles.apply: Consider using a secondary ball to limit travel only when the resulting table and legality are understood.
principles.exceptions: Unintended contact is not equivalent; it may alter the finish or create a foul.
principles.check: What happens to both balls after contact and is the continuation still valid?

principles.title: Pocket-entry variation can create an otherwise unavailable route
principles.apply: Consider a feasible entry offset when it changes cue-ball departure usefully.
principles.exceptions: This reduces pot margin; pocket geometry and speed must validate it. It is an advanced option, not a default fix.
principles.check: Does the recovered position justify the narrower pot margin?

principles.title: A rail-first approach to a hanger can change the cue-ball exit
principles.apply: Consider cushion-before-object contact when a near-pocket ball offers a useful alternate exit.
principles.exceptions: This is not an object-ball bank; confirm clearance, first object contact and applicable rules.
principles.check: Does the rail-first route produce a useful exit with adequate pot margin?

principles.title: Distinguish setup freedom from an ongoing rack
principles.apply: When a drill grants ball in hand, choose an opening that establishes the pattern; preserve actual cue-ball position during an ongoing run.
principles.exceptions: Book exercises granting ball in hand do not grant it in a player's live game.
principles.check: Is placement freedom actually part of this situation?

principles.title: Use constraints to isolate cue-ball control
principles.apply: Offer optional practice limiting side spin or table area to develop rolling and sliding control.
principles.exceptions: The source's half-table restriction is an exercise condition, not a general strategic rule.
principles.check: Which constraint teaches the intended skill without confusing normal play?

principles.title: Reveal a small useful hint before the entire explanation when wanted
principles.apply: Offer the opening idea or a decisive transition as optional scaffolding, then let the player explore.
principles.exceptions: Direct questions deserve direct answers; do not force guessing or conceal requested help.
principles.check: Does the player want exploration, a hint or an explanation?

principles.title: Interpret difficulty relative to task family
principles.apply: Distinguish task length and type from within-family difficulty; do not compare source skill meters as absolute ratings.
principles.exceptions: No player rating or success percentage follows from a printed difficulty gauge.
principles.check: What aspect of the task is demanding for this player?

principles.title: Treat source spin illustrations as qualitative starting guidance
principles.apply: Account for cue, table, stroke and starting-position differences before transferring settings.
principles.exceptions: The author reports testing the patterns; that does not calibrate exact Trainer inputs or real-table guarantees.
principles.check: Which conditions differ from the demonstration?

principles.title: Last-pocket play changes the finishing constraint
principles.apply: When that variant is selected, plan the final group-ball pocket jointly with the required winning-ball pocket.
principles.exceptions: Do not impose this exercise rule on standard 8-ball; verify the selected variant.
principles.check: Does the complete finish obey the chosen same-pocket constraint?

principles.title: A defensive option must consider both balls' destinations
principles.apply: From the defensive diagrams, assess cue-ball separation and the legal target ball's resulting access together.
principles.exceptions: The diagrams show candidates, not universally successful safeties or computed opponent odds.
principles.check: What reasonable return does the opponent retain?

principles.title: A legal hit alone may not solve the strategic problem
principles.apply: Compare the likely opponent opportunity after a difficult escape with alternatives, rather than treating contact as the only goal.
principles.exceptions: Do not invent opponent runout probabilities or claim a foul is harmless.
principles.check: What changes in the opponent's practical options after this choice?

principles.title: A deliberate foul is a separately labeled strategic tradeoff
principles.apply: If discussing the source's tie-up choices, explicitly identify the foul and ball-in-hand concession and compare legal options first.
principles.exceptions: Confirm the actual rules and any consecutive-foul penalty before recommending; never label it a legal runout continuation.
principles.check: Does the obstruction created plausibly justify the known penalty under these rules?

principles.title: Keep defence separate from offensive pattern verification
principles.apply: When no attractive offensive route is established, distinguish a safety search from a runout claim.
principles.exceptions: A failed bounded runout search is not proof that no runout exists.
principles.check: Which objective is being evaluated and what evidence supports it?

principles.title: Inspect the full cue-ball path, not only the endpoint.
principles.apply: Inspect scratch risk along the full cue-ball trajectory, including side-pocket mouths, jaws, blockers and unintended collisions; compare tested alternatives.
principles.exceptions: A close visual pass is a warning, not measured scratch probability.
principles.check: What observed or computed evidence supports this statement?

principles.title: Distinguish nominal success from tolerance.
principles.apply: Perturb plausible aim, speed and tip placement before calling a route forgiving.
principles.exceptions: An arbitrary drawn region and one nominal success do not establish tolerance.
principles.check: What observed or computed evidence supports this statement?

principles.title: Only recorded tool results support verification.
principles.apply: Tie computed claims to actual tool inputs, results and starting snapshot.
principles.exceptions: Do not invent tests or retract genuine evidence merely because the recommendation was poor.
principles.check: What observed or computed evidence supports this statement?

principles.title: Preserve every ball in successor states.
principles.apply: Chain verified final states without repositioning balls; replan from actual results after execution.
principles.exceptions: Independent preview_shot calls do not prove a runout; use simulate_shot successor states or a recorded search_runout replay.
principles.check: What observed or computed evidence supports this statement?

principles.title: Describe search coverage precisely.
principles.apply: Report checked depth, alternatives and budget limits.
principles.exceptions: Best found is not a global optimum; no solution found is not impossibility.
principles.check: What observed or computed evidence supports this statement?

principles.title: Do not overgeneralize this source.
principles.apply: Separate pattern-play abstractions, defensive diagrams, drill constraints and app safeguards.
principles.exceptions: The source excludes banks/combinations from pattern puzzles; defensive interludes include other objectives.
principles.check: What observed or computed evidence supports this statement?

principles.title: Use diagrams as evidence with uncertainty.
principles.apply: Check labels, ball roles, route keys and text together; explain ambiguity instead of fabricating calibrated values.
principles.exceptions: Cue-ball numbers can denote shot sequence; black obstacle symbols need not be the 8 ball.
principles.check: What observed or computed evidence supports this statement?

principles.title: Match the explanation to the player request.
principles.apply: Give the decisive reason and an optional next cue; expand when requested.
principles.exceptions: Do not dump the principle catalog or require logging and interrogation.
principles.check: What observed or computed evidence supports this statement?
